question_bank.stem: After prompt engineering, a team asks whether it should fine-tune a general model for a new task. Which caution from the lecture most strongly argues against routine fine-tuning?

options.text: The effort can be time- and cost-intensive, and a newer base model may surpass the fine-tuned version before the work pays off.
The effort automatically removes all domain-specific behavior, so repeated specialized tasks become harder to solve.
The effort prevents any future prompting, so the model can no longer adapt to different instructions at inference time.
The effort forces the system to abandon pretraining entirely, so the model must relearn general language from scratch.

question_bank.rationale: The instructor's main practical objection is that fine-tuning can take time and money while the next base model may arrive and outperform it.

source_ref.evidence_span: the next model is out, and it's actually

frame_evidence.visual_description: Slide titled Why I'm not a fan lists fine-tuning limitations including labeled-data needs, overfitting risk, and high time or cost.

question_bank.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes prompting from fine-tuning in the lecture?

options.text: Fine-tuning changes the prompt template, whereas prompting permanently updates the model weights.
Fine-tuning changes model weights, whereas prompting changes the context without modifying the weights.
Fine-tuning changes only the tokenizer, whereas prompting changes the optimizer state during inference.
Fine-tuning changes only the retrieval index, whereas prompting replaces the decoder with a judge model.

question_bank.rationale: The lecture explicitly contrasts fine-tuning with approaches that do not modify the weights.

source_ref.evidence_span: the other doesn't modify the weights.

frame_evidence.visual_description: Fine-tuning section is on screen while the instructor verbally contrasts weight updates with prompt-only methods.

question_bank.stem: A company fine-tunes on internal Slack messages, then asks the model to draft a blog post and gets a workplace-style reply instead. What failure mode does this example illustrate?

options.text: The model loses all ability to produce text longer than a chat reply because fine-tuning fixes the output length.
The model stops understanding prompts entirely because Slack data removes instruction-following behavior from the architecture.
The model can overfit to the tone and habits of the fine-tuning data instead of performing the requested task well.
The model becomes impossible to deploy because any fine-tuned model can only answer inside Slack after training.

question_bank.rationale: The Slack example shows the model imitating how coworkers talk instead of reliably doing the requested writing task.

source_ref.evidence_span: where Ros tried to do Slack fine tuning.

frame_evidence.visual_description: Slide titled Example: Slack Fine-Tuning shows a prompt for a blog post and a Slack-like response promising to work on it in the morning.

question_bank.stem: Which scenario did the lecture present as a more defensible case for fine-tuning?

options.text: A broad general-purpose assistant that mostly needs fresher news and access to the latest documents.
A short-lived prototype where the main goal is to explore product ideas before investing in infrastructure.
A workflow that mainly fails because the retrieved evidence is missing from the context window.
A repeated high-precision task with domain-specific language, such as specialized legal or scientific outputs.

question_bank.rationale: The lecture says fine-tuning can still make sense for repeated high-precision tasks or strong domain-language mismatches.

frame_evidence.visual_description: Fine-tuning section continues while the instructor gives niche cases where specialized language might justify the extra effort.
